meta.tagline: Canals, a belfry and a medieval fairytale that smells of chocolate

pills: A medieval city left as it was

overview.title: Welcome to Bruges
overview.intro: Bruges was once Europe's richest port; then its link to the sea silted up, the trade left, and the city fell asleep for five centuries. That sleep turned into a miracle: nobody tore it down to build anew, and the Middle Ages simply stayed. Today swans drift along the canals, the belfry plays its melody on the hour, and every step you take on the cobbles lands inside a postcard. The crowds arrive by day and sail off by evening — you stay; Bruges shows its true face at night.

local_word.definition: Literally 'Burgundian', but for the Flemish it's a philosophy of life: good food, good beer, a long table and enjoying it all without guilt. It's the answer to why a dinner in Bruges takes three hours.

rules.title: Spend the night here
rules.description: Day-trippers see only the city's crowds. When the tours leave at five, the canal banks empty and the stone streets are yours — an overnight stay is this city's real ticket.

rules.title: Beer is drunk from its own glass
rules.description: Every Belgian beer has its own glass, and this is no joke: the bartender will make you wait if the right glass is in the wash. Pick a beer you've never heard of from the menu, and respect its glass.

rules.title: Choose chocolate by the maker, not the window
rules.description: The city has more than fifty chocolate shops; some sell factory chocolate as handmade. Go where you see the 'chocolatier' crest and a working kitchen in the shop.

quick_facts.label: Getting there
quick_facts.sub: Station to centre 15 min on foot

quick_facts.label: Getting around
quick_facts.sub: Centre end to end in 25 minutes

tip.label: The Bruges philosophy
tip.text: Don't plan in Bruges; put the map in your pocket and get lost. The city is small, and every wrong street ends at either a canal or a square — both count as a win.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The centre of Bruges is a medieval island closed to cars; the fastest vehicle is your own feet, the most enjoyable a bicycle.

items.title: Arriving by train
items.description: Several trains an hour from Brussels, roughly a one-hour ride. Walk from the station to the centre through Minnewater park: you'll enter the city through its most beautiful gate.

items.title: Everywhere on foot
items.description: No walk from the Markt to the farthest corner takes more than 25 minutes. Cobblestones are the enemy of heels; wear comfortable soles and keep your eyes on the gables.

items.title: The ramparts by bike
items.description: Rent a bike and circle the old rampart line (the Vesten): windmills, gate towers and a green path along the canal. Pedalling the canalside to Damme is the best half-day investment there is.

items.title: The canal boat
items.description: The half-hour boat tour shows the city from water level: under the bridges, hidden gardens, façades you can't see any other way. Touristy, but deservedly so — take the first departure of the morning.

items.title: Airport connections
items.description: The most practical route is the direct train from Brussels Airport; landing at Charleroi means a bus-plus-train combination. Either way: ticket from the machine, change in Brussels.

callout.label: Morning tip
callout.text: The first canal boats and the Rozenhoedkaai quay are nearly empty before 9 am; take your postcard photo before anyone arrives, and have breakfast afterwards.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Distances in Bruges are small; the difference is atmosphere: canalside romance, square-side buzz or neighbourhood calm?

local_word.definition: Whitewashed almshouses built by rich guilds for the poor; walled gardens, deep quiet, most still inhabited. If the gate is open you may quietly peek into the garden — these are Bruges' most peaceful courtyards.

items.name: Around the Markt and Burg
items.description: For those who want to wake in the belfry's shadow: everything is outside your door, and early mornings and late nights are magical. Daytime crowds and square noise are part of the bargain.

items.name: Rozenhoedkaai and the canalside
items.description: Historic mansion hotels facing the canal: swans outside the window in the morning, silence on the stone quay at night. The honeymoon and anniversary classic; prices scale with the view.

items.name: Sint-Anna quarter
items.description: A calm neighbourhood ten minutes east of the centre: next door to the windmills, low on tourists, with warm-hearted guesthouses. The real Bruges morning happens here.

items.name: Minnewater and the Begijnhof area
items.description: Beside the 'Lake of Love' and the beguinage: swans, willows and evening stillness. Near the station — practical with a suitcase — and next to the park, a gift for morning runners.

items.name: The Ezelstraat area
items.description: A calm axis of galleries and shops northwest of the centre: ten minutes to the Markt, prices a notch friendlier. The territory of boutique hotels and small design guesthouses.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Bruges is a postcard in every season; only the colour of the light and the thickness of the crowds change.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Daffodil Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Flowering courtyards, mild canal cruises
items.description: The Minnewater and the godshuis gardens burst into flower, the terraces go up, and the canal boats open their finest season. The crowds grow, but the city still breathes.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: On Ascension Day (May/June) the Heilig Bloedprocessie takes place: the whole city carries the relic of the Holy Blood through the streets in medieval costume — Bruges' oldest day.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Long Evenings
items.subtitle: Summer · Light until 10 pm, terraces full
items.description: The days are long and the canalside terraces live late into the evening; the daytime crowds are at their peak. The formula is simple: out early in the morning, into a museum at midday, take the city back at night.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: Day-trip crowds peak between 11 am and 5 pm; use those hours for Sint-Anna, the windmills and the museums, and save the squares for morning and evening.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Mist and Golden Leaves
items.subtitle: Autumn · Misty canals, quiet streets
items.description: Morning mist settles on the canals, leaves float on the water, and the city wears its most photogenic melancholy. The crowds recede and hotel prices soften — this is the photographer's season.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: In November the fireplaces of the beer cafés are lit: mist outside, a dark quadrupel inside — a winter rehearsal of the Bourgondisch life.

items.label: Winter
items.name: A Christmas Tale
items.subtitle: Winter · Christmas market, ice rink, hot chocolate
items.description: A Christmas market and ice rink fill the Markt and the gables are wrapped in light; January and February are the city at its emptiest and quietest — the season for walking the canals alone.

callout.label: December tip
callout.text: Visit the Christmas market on a weekday evening and look up at the lit belfry with a hot chocolate in hand: there is no option left but to admit you live inside a postcard.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Flemish cooking is hearty and proud: they invented frites, turned beer into an art form, and raised the chocolate bar to the sky.

local_word.definition: A frites stand: one of Belgium's national institutions. The potatoes are fried twice, served in a paper cone, and choosing the sauce is a serious decision. Never say 'French fries' in Belgium — the invention is theirs.

items.name: Frites — in a cone, double-fried
items.description: Real Belgian frites are fried twice: crisp outside, creamy inside. Take your cone, choose andalouse or classic mayonnaise on top, and eat them standing by a canal.
items.tag: From a frietkot · be brave with the sauce

items.name: Vlaamse stoofvlees — beef braised in beer
items.description: Beef stewed for hours in dark Belgian beer: frites alongside, the beer's caramel on top. The heart of Flemish cooking is this pot.
items.tag: At a local tavern · frites are mandatory

items.name: Moules-frites in season
items.description: From September to April the mussel pots arrive: white wine, celery, thyme. The pot lid becomes your plate and an empty shell your tongs — you learn the technique at the table.
items.tag: Sep–Apr · in the months with an 'r'

items.name: The Belgian waffle — two schools
items.description: The Brussels waffle is rectangular and light, the Liège waffle dense and caramelised. The tourist version comes buried under fruit; locals eat theirs plain or with icing sugar only.
items.tag: Hot and plain · no mountain of toppings needed

items.name: Master-made pralines
items.description: The Belgians invented the praline, and in Bruges' back-street workshops they are still poured by hand. Have a box filled with a mix — and don't skip the sea-salt caramel.
items.tag: From a handmade chocolatier · mix the box

items.name: Brugse Zot and its Trappist big brothers
items.description: The city's own beer, Brugse Zot, means 'the fool of Bruges'; the legend behind it is the city's nickname. If the beer menu overwhelms you, describe your taste to the bartender — the right beer arrives in the right glass.
items.tag: In its own glass · ask the bartender

callout.label: The beer rule
callout.text: Belgian beer is like wine: it starts at 6 percent and climbs to 12. Trappists and quadrupels are drunk sitting down — not before getting on a bike, and not after either.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone photographs the Rozenhoedkaai; these six are the Bruges two streets behind the crowd.

items.name: Jeruzalemkapel
items.description: The strange and mesmerising chapel built in the 15th century by the Adornes family after their pilgrimage to Jerusalem: a replica of Golgotha, a tomb chamber, an intact family inheritance. Still owned by the same family — nothing like it in Europe.

items.name: The Kruisvest windmills
items.description: Four windmills line a green ridge along the old rampart; one still grinds flour. Canal, sails and grass — a view that demands a picnic blanket.

items.name: The Begijnhof
items.description: Whitewashed beguine houses standing since 1245 around a poplar-shaded court: voices drop by themselves as you pass the gate. In spring the lawn becomes a carpet of daffodils.

items.name: The De Halve Maan beer pipeline
items.description: The city's historic brewery laid a three-kilometre underground beer pipeline to its bottling plant to get trucks off the cobbles: the tour ends on a rooftop terrace with a view, tasting included.

items.rarity: The prettiest canal, the fewest people
items.name: The Groenerei quay
items.description: With its ivy-clad stone bridges and trees leaning over the water, this is the city's most graceful stretch of canal; tour boats pass, but the walking crowds rarely turn this way. Walk it in late-afternoon light.

items.name: Cycling to Damme
items.description: A flat, poplar-lined canal path drops you in the medieval town of Damme in half an hour: bookshops, a single square, a Gothic town hall. The wind always blows against you on the way back — set out knowing it.

callout.label: Tower tip
callout.text: If the Belfort queue is long, go to Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk instead: Michelangelo's Bruges Madonna is there, with hardly any queue at all. When the only Michelangelo sculpture ever to leave Rome is two steps away, the tower photo can wait.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Bruges is a small and honest city; its traps are small too, but they aim squarely at the day-trip crowd.

items.name: 'Handmade' chocolate with a fancy window
items.description: Some shops around the Markt sell factory chocolate in tourist wrapping at triple the price; a chocolate fountain and giant moulds in the window do not mean production.
items.instead: Go to real chocolatiers with a visible workshop: back-street shops bearing the maker's name give you hand-poured pralines for the same money.

items.name: The menu boards facing the Markt
items.description: Most restaurants with a square view add the view to the bill: lukewarm mussels, reheated stoofvlees, a tourist menu.
items.instead: Walk two streets back; the small taverns around Sint-Amandsstraat and Ezelstraat make the same dishes fresh, at half the price.

items.name: Squeezing the city into 11 am–4 pm
items.description: Day-trippers see Bruges in its five most crowded hours and go home calling it 'too touristy'; the city isn't at fault, the clock is.
items.instead: Stay a night: the canals at 8 am and the lit square at 10 pm belong to you alone. Bruges' real show runs outside office hours.

items.name: A carriage ride after a long queue
items.description: The carriages on the square have fixed prices, but at peak hours you wait in line and the tired horses run a weary routine.
items.instead: Walk the same route — the city was built for walking. If you love horses, take the first tour of the morning: the horses are fresh and the streets empty.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Bruges, turn away from wherever the crowd is looking: the finest gables, the best taverns and the calmest canals are always two streets behind the square.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A medieval tale that begins with morning mist

steps.title: The empty squares
steps.description: The Markt and the Burg before the tourists: the belfry, the guild façades and the cobbles are yours alone. Drink your coffee at the edge of the square.

steps.title: Canal boat + Rozenhoedkaai
steps.description: A boat tour on one of the first departures, then the classic postcard shot from the quay; don't forget to greet the swans.

steps.title: A frietkot stop and the Madonna
steps.description: Frites in a cone for a standing lunch; then Michelangelo's Bruges Madonna at Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk — five minutes of silence is enough.

steps.title: Begijnhof and Minnewater
steps.description: A quiet loop of the white courtyard, then willow shade beside the Lake of Love: the city's pulse slows down here.

steps.title: From the Groenerei to Sint-Anna
steps.description: Walk the loveliest stretch of canal into the calm quarter and on to the windmills: the crowds are already behind you.

steps.title: Stoofvlees + a beer to close
steps.description: Beer-braised stew at a neighbourhood tavern, then a quadrupel in a historic beer café: a Bourgondisch ending.

steps.title: Classic Bruges
steps.description: The one-day flow above: squares, boat, Madonna, Begijnhof, canal walk, beer.

steps.title: Museums and workshops
steps.description: Flemish masters at the Groeningemuseum in the morning, then the Jeruzalemkapel and the lace centre; the De Halve Maan brewery tour in the afternoon, moules-frites in the evening (if in season).

steps.title: Bicycle and farewell
steps.description: Pedal the canal to Damme, take a long lunch in the town; on the way back, the Kruisvest windmills and one last box of chocolates — not the only souvenir going home in your suitcase.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Bruges speaks Dutch; everyone knows English, but these five words open doors with a smile.

items.meaning: Good day — said as you enter a shop, always returned
Thank you — 'dank u' works for short
Please / here you go — the waiter sets your plate down with it, and you order with it
Cheers! — the Flemish also say 'schol'; eye contact is mandatory
Delicious / great — the day's most-used word, for frites and beer alike

checklist.title: Bruges Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Schol! You've lived the Bruges fairytale properly!

items.sub: After 6 pm the city belongs to those who stay
